I’m really glad you brought that up—that’s a lovely way to use the space, and a nice way to keep a bit of that connection going too.

And yes, container gardening is actually perfect for a balcony and very beginner-friendly if you keep it simple.

If you’re just starting out, herbs are the easiest and most rewarding place to begin. They don’t need much space, and you can actually use them in your cooking right away. Good starter choices are things like basil, mint, parsley, chives, or thyme. Basil especially does well in good sunlight, and mint is very forgiving (almost too forgiving—it likes to take over its pot).

A few basics to keep in mind, without overcomplicating it:

- Sunlight: Most herbs and vegetables like a good amount of sun—ideally 5–7 hours a day. If your balcony gets that, you’re in great shape.
- Pots: Anything with drainage holes works. That’s more important than the pot itself—plants don’t like sitting in soggy soil.
- Soil: Use potting mix rather than garden soil. It’s lighter and drains better.
- Watering: This is where most beginners get tripped up. You don’t want bone-dry soil, but you also don’t want it constantly soaked. A simple trick is to stick your finger into the soil—if the top inch feels dry, it’s time to water.

If you want to try a vegetable, something like cherry tomatoes or lettuce can work well in containers. Cherry tomatoes especially can be quite satisfying—you get a steady little harvest once they get going.

One other gentle tip: start small. Maybe 2–4 plants to begin with. It’s much more enjoyable to succeed with a few than to feel like you’re managing a whole garden right away.

If you’d like, you can tell me roughly which direction your balcony faces (north, south, etc.), and I can suggest a few plants that would suit it really well.

It’s lighter and drains well. Regular garden soil (the kind you’d dig into in a yard) is actually too dense for pots and can lead to water sitting around the roots, which plants don’t like.

You don’t need anything fancy or expensive—just a basic potting mix is perfectly fine for herbs.

- Parsley: similar, around 8 inches or so

If a pot seems a bit bigger than necessary, that’s usually okay—it gives the roots room and means you won’t have to repot as quickly. The key thing, again, is making sure there’s a hole at the bottom so excess water can drain out.
